newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia mulls changes in draft privatisation law.
newsitem.headline: Serbia mulls changes in draft privatisation law.

text.p: Serbia is mulling changes in its draft privatisation law to make it legally more precise and socially fair and to include more people in the process, a Serbian official said on Tuesday.

"The government is considering the possibility of including even more people in the privatisation process and giving the right to farmers, private entrepreneurs and Yugoslav workers employed abroad to take part," Mirouljub Hadzic, assistant to the Serbian Privatisation Minister, told Reuters.
Initially, the government said up to four million people would take part in the process, including all employees who had ever worked in the state sector, pensioners and state administration workers.
But the first draft privatisation law did not include those who had always been private sector employees or Yugoslavs working abroad.
The ministry will also give more equal access to domestic and foreign investors by granting them nearly the same level of discounts for purchasing shares, Hadzic told a meeting of private businesses.

According to the current version of the document, subject to a month-long public debate, workers are offered a 70 percent discount up to a total dinar equivalent of 20,000 German marks ($11,500) in subscribed shares.

Along with simplifying legal terminology in the document, the privatisation ministry is looking into the possibility of making the process compulsory for all companies and defining a specific time-frame.
Law makers will have to reconsider where and in which percentages to direct privatisation receipts.

According to the draft, 50 percent of privatisation proceeds are planned for the Serbian Development Fund, with 25 percent each to the Serbian Pension Fund and the Serbian Labour Office for creating new jobs.

But the law did not precisely tackle the issue of hard currency savings, frozen in state banks since 1991, except for introducing the possibility that holders of those savings should take part in the second stage of the privatisation process.
Meanwhile, some bankers called on the government to direct 25 percent of all privatisation receipts to a fund which will repay the debt.
According to the latest official estimates, the state owes its citizens 6.7 billion German marks in frozen savings together with accumulated interest.
"It is an arbitrary decision on how much money to direct to any of those funds," Hadzic said and added that parliament might seek even more privatisation cash for pension funds.

However, the concept offered by the government rejected voucher privatisation and did not tackle restitution, which many opposition political parties and private businesses saw as the key to establishing a proper and secure investment climate.

Members of the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce's Department for Private Enterprise called on the state to return all assets to original owners, create a better environment for fair market competition, launch a stable fiscal system and introduce more protection for investors.

"If the state does not do this, the privatisation law will remain good only for political marketing purposes ahead of the elections," said Dragutin Zagorac, president of the Serbian Employers Confederation.
Defending the draft law, Hadzic said the government had no intention of avoiding the issue of restitution.
"If restitution were included in this law, we would have to wait several years to really begin with privatisation," Hadzic said.
